description: Behavioral conformance vectors for the seven-mode retry-safety battery named in x402-foundation/x402#3208 (aurumflux20, https://aurumflux.co/retry-safety/): accept_then_timeout, 5xx_after_settle, double_402, slow_answer, reconcile_unavailable, declared_safe, clean. Unlike the hash-derivation vectors elsewhere in this directory (offer-identity-ref, settlement-evidence-ref), these are behavioral: each vector names a mode and the expected outcome of actually running execute_payment() against MockFacilitator in that mode, not a static artifact hash. A conformant implementation reproduces the same terminal verdict and the same ledger_len==1 for every positive vector, by running the code, not by reading the spec.
comparator_rule: PASS requires: running execute_payment() in a caller retry loop (bounded, MAX_ROUNDS=5) against MockFacilitator(mode) reaches final_verdict=='settled' with the facilitator's ledger holding exactly one entry (ledger_len==1) for that authorization. mutation-broken-client-001 is a negative control: it is expected to FAIL (ledger_len>1) precisely because it violates the rule under test (it mints a new authorization on every retry instead of re-presenting the same one) — its purpose is to prove the comparator discriminates, not to pass.

source.receiver_obligation_text: an indeterminate state explicitly locks the invoice and preserves the broadcast hash until deterministic reconciliation completes. A normative clause stating that receivers MUST NOT re-challenge a pending authorization is essential to make third-party implementations safe by default.

vectors.description: Baseline: single settle() call succeeds on the first attempt, no fault.

Facilitator settles on first attempt AND a duplicate client-side submission of the same idempotency_key (simulating an accidental double-send, not a fault-triggered retry) must still settle exactly once — the 'exactly once there too' clause aurumflux20's proposal names for this mode specifically.

First settle() call broadcasts (facilitator ledger written) but the receipt-wait times out before the client sees it — the #3083 pattern: broadcast ref IS surfaced in the exception. Client reconciles by that ref on the next round instead of re-settling blind.

First settle() call broadcasts, then the facilitator 500s with no broadcast ref in the body (the ref-based reconcile path is unavailable to the client). Client re-presents the SAME authorization on retry; facilitator-side signature dedup returns the already-settled transaction instead of writing a second entry.

First settle() call broadcasts, but the client's own timeout fires before any response (server-side success, client-side loss) — no ref available to the client, same re-presentation path as 5xx_after_settle.

First settle() call broadcasts and times out with a ref surfaced, but the reconcile query against that ref itself fails on the first attempt. Client falls back to re-presenting the same authorization; facilitator-side dedup (not reconcile) is what actually closes it.

First settle() call times out with no broadcast yet. Second call: the facilitator re-challenges with a fresh 402 instead of resuming the pending authorization — the exact hazard whawk46's MUST-NOT-re-challenge clause targets. Client MUST NOT sign a new authorization to satisfy the new challenge; it re-presents the original signed authorization directly, which the facilitator then settles.

Negative control, not a mode from the battery. A deliberately broken client that mints a NEW authorization signature on every retry (violating the re-presentation rule) run against the same double_402 facilitator. Must produce a real double charge (ledger_len==2) to prove the PASS vectors above are discriminating and not a facilitator mock that always settles once regardless of client behavior. Reproducible: see verify.py's run_mutation_control().
